text: Dot matrix printing, also known as impact matrix printing, is a computer printing process that applies ink to a surface using a low-resolution dot matrix layout. It is a type of impact printer that uses a fixed number of pins or wires in a print head that moves back and forth or up and down, striking an ink-soaked cloth ribbon against the paper to create printed output. Unlike typewriters or line printers that only produce specific characters, dot matrix printers can print arbitrary patterns and custom graphics. The quality of the print depends on vertical and horizontal resolution and the ability of the printer to overlap adjacent dots; common configurations include 9-pin and 24-pin models, with 24-pin printers offering better visual quality—referred to as near letter-quality (NLQ)—through overlapping dots, though at the cost of speed. These printers are distinguished from non-impact technologies like inkjet, thermal, or laser printing, which also use bitmaps but offer higher resolution, faster speeds, and quieter operation. Impact printers can print on multi-part forms, enabling multiple copies simultaneously, and use continuous fanfold paper with perforated tractor holes for easy page separation. In 1925, Rudolf Hell invented the Hellschreiber, an early dot matrix-based teletypewriter, patented in 1929. Between 1952 and 1954, Fritz Karl Preikschat filed five patent applications for his "PKT printer," a dot matrix teletypewriter built between 1954 and 1956 in Germany, which used asynchronous transmission instead of synchronous transmission. In 1956, it was offered to the Deutsche Bundespost, which showed no interest; after Preikschat emigrated to the US in 1957, he sold the rights (except in the USA) to Telefonbau und Normalzeit GmbH (TuN), and the prototype was shown to General Mills in 1957. A transistorized version became the basis for a portable dot matrix facsimile machine, prototyped and evaluated by Boeing around 1966–1967. In 1968, OKI introduced the OKI Wiredot, the first serial impact dot matrix printer (SIDM), supporting 128 characters with a 7 × 5 print matrix, targeting governmental, financial, scientific, and educational markets; OKI received an award from the Information Processing Society of Japan (IPSJ) in 2013. In 1970, Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) introduced the LA30, a 30 character per second (CPS) dot matrix printer, and Centronics (then of Hudson, New Hampshire) introduced the Centronics 101. Centronics developed a parallel interface that became standard until replaced by USB in the late 1990s. DEC focused on its PDP minicomputer line, and the LA30 was available with both parallel and serial interfaces, with the serial version requiring fill characters during carriage return; a receive-only version, LA30A, was introduced in 1972. In 1974, the LA36 succeeded the LA30, achieving greater commercial success and becoming a standard terminal; it supported up to 132 columns of mixed-case output on green bar fanfold paper, used a servo drive with DC motor and optical encoder, and had no fill characters due to buffering during carriage return, producing a distinctive two-tone buzz from 60 CPS catch-up printing followed by 30 CPS normal printing—a feature widely copied by other manufacturers. The LA50, another DEC model, could generate graphics in bitmap mode using the Sixel format. The Centronics 101 was innovative and affordable, with specifications including 80 columns and 120 CPS. The IBM 5103 was the only IBM printer compatible with the IBM 5100 portable computer, offering 8 DPI, 10 pitch, 6 LPI, and bidirectional printing from a 128-character set at 80 or 120 CPS. Near Letter Quality (NLQ) mode, which simulated typewriter-like output through multiple passes and higher dot density, was informally described in 1985 by The New York Times as "a neat little bit of hype" but acknowledged its strengths in fonts and graphics. NLQ printers could also operate in draft mode, using a single pass for faster output. In 1985, PC Magazine stated that dot matrix remained the most workable choice for average users, and IBM sold Epson's MX-80 as the IBM 5152. Early dot matrix printers like the Epson TX-80 (1978) and MX-80/MP-80 (1979–1980) boosted popularity in the personal computer market due to affordability and decent text output, though they were loud and had low dot density (60 dpi horizontal, 72 dpi vertical), resulting in a "computerized" appearance and poor legibility compared to daisy-wheel printers. Output quality degraded with photocopying, and third-party software offered fixes. In 1981, Epson introduced a Graftrax EPROM kit to enable bitmap image printing on MX series printers, leading to widespread use of banners and signs in offices and schools. As dot density and carriage speed increased (up to 240 dpi), printers supported proportional fonts and user-downloadable custom typefaces, allowing up to two NLQ fonts to be stored. The desktop impact printer was gradually replaced by inkjet printers, which became available after Hewlett-Packard's US patent on steam-propelled photolithographic ink-jet heads expired in 2004. Inkjet printers were superior in quiet operation, speed, and print quality, surpassing dot matrix by 1995 and relegating it to niche uses. As of 2021, dot matrix impact technology is still used in applications such as multi-part stationery at bank tellers and auto repair shops, data logging, and aviation, where tractor feed paper is preferred. Most modern dot matrix printers now include USB interfaces for compatibility with contemporary computers.
